name: Full Node
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: The Participants Who Trust No One
lesson.summary: A full node is a node that downloads and independently verifies the entire blockchain history against the network's rules, rather than trusting other participants for any part of that verification, making full nodes the backbone of a blockchain's trustlessness.
lesson.body:
The previous section noted that nodes vary in how much they store and verify, and promised a closer look at the category that does the most work: full nodes. A full node downloads the entire history of the blockchain, every block since the genesis block, and independently checks every single rule the network defines: that every transaction's signature is valid, that no funds are double spent, that every block's header correctly references the one before it, and that every block follows the consensus rules for how blocks are allowed to be created. A full node trusts no other participant's word for any of this. It verifies everything itself, from scratch, using only the rules encoded in its own software.

This is where the earlier sections in this chapter converge into a single practical activity. Recall the block header discussion: a full node checks that each header's previous hash field correctly links to the prior block, exactly as described there. Recall transaction validation: a full node performs that exact check, signature by signature, for every transaction in every block, not just the ones it happens to care about. Recall the genesis block: a full node's very first act on joining the network is confirming the chain it is downloading traces back to the exact, hardcoded genesis block its software expects, rejecting any chain that does not.

The value of running one is mostly about not having to trust anyone else. If you rely on someone else's server to tell you your balance, or whether a payment you received is genuine, you are trusting that server's honesty and correctness, which is precisely the kind of single point of trust a distributed ledger was supposed to remove in the first place, as discussed at the start of this chapter. Running a full node means verifying, with your own hardware and the network's public rules, that a payment sent to you is real, was properly signed, was not double spent, and sits inside a block that correctly follows the entire chain of valid blocks back to genesis, without asking anyone to vouch for any of it.

This comes at a real cost, which is worth stating plainly rather than glossing over. A full node needs enough storage to hold the entire blockchain history, which for established networks can run into the hundreds of gigabytes and grows continuously, since the append-only design discussed earlier in this chapter guarantees the record only ever gets bigger, never smaller. It also needs meaningful bandwidth to receive and relay data to its peers, and enough processing power to check every signature and every rule for every historical block during initial setup, a process that can take days on ordinary consumer hardware. This is precisely the cost that pushes many users toward lighter nodes or third party services instead, echoing the centralization concern raised in the previous section.

The honest summary is that full nodes are where a blockchain's abstract promises, immutability, trustlessness, censorship resistance, actually get cashed out into concrete, checkable computation. A network's rules are only as meaningful as the number of independent parties actually enforcing them by running full nodes. A blockchain with a beautiful, tamper evident hash chain design but almost nobody actually verifying it end to end is trustworthy mostly in theory. Full nodes are what make the theory something you can personally rely on, without asking anyone's permission or believing anyone's claim.
